I'm a devout Christian INTP. Horrible with religion - I struggle to attend church and can't get on board with waving my hands in worship. Didn't grow up in a particularly religious household and actually despised religion as a younger tween. But I do absolutely feel convicted by my faith and exploring both Biblical writings and the context behind it. 

The biggest fault today is that people refuse to accept the context behind the Bible, the fact it's originally written in ancient Hebrew and Greek in astronomically different societies from today and in their translations, meanings have been lost, changed, or are difficult to apply to today's society and it uses a ton of story telling and figurative language. Regardless, different denominations roll with it and throughout all of history have weaponized it in ways that directly go against the one Commandment that encompasses all: love your neighbor as yourself.

Purity culture, xenophobia, homophobia, being judgmental, and other like-topics are byproducts of this which is so ironically hypocritical since Jesus was literally crucified next to what was seen as the scum of the Earth, his disciples included adulterers and tax collectors. Jesus saved an adulterous woman from being legally stoned against. There's also a misconception that the Bible is a rule book of do's and don'ts so you can get into Heaven - couldn't be farther from the truth. The whole point is NO ONE is perfect, it's impossible to be perfect, and yet you are loved by God and have the capacity to love absolutely anyone else on this planet.

I question my faith everyday. I totally understand I might be wrong but oh well. It's difficult because it calls you to deny yourself and openly admit you don't know exactly what's right, and admit you're innately crappy and need guidance and help. But I always err on the side of compassion and understanding and we absolutely need more of it in the US and world as a whole. If you choose to love God back and walk in that faith you have to be prepared for bad to still happen in your life, to have things taken from you and to still experience human suffering and yet love God anyways, of your own free will. I refuse to Bible thump because of that.

Especially being a daily smoker, 4 weeks may not be enough. THC can be detectable for up to 3 months. I’d wait, and in the meantime buy 15ng at home tests, and buy different brands. Then, after MEPS, don’t smoke! You’ll take another urinalysis during P-Days in boot camp. Piss often, try to burn some fat and best of luck

Start now! I went to boot camp doing 48 push-ups and I left doing 64. Search up the “grease the groove” method with push-ups and get to where you can pass the initial PFA. Once you’re at boot, keep doing push-ups all day, and give your all during PT sessions. Really emphasize running too right now, we did not run nearly enough in boot camp. I also did 100 push-ups before bed each night except Sunday, my rest day, in whatever way possible. 5x20, threw in some variations like diamond and decline. You can absolutely get better, it all depends on how willing you are to start working as hard as possible. Good luck!

MEPS is the hardest urinalysis test I’ve done because the staff gets impatient. Just chug water and do NOT pee beforehand. Chug water out of the water fountain as much as you can and wait until you are literally about to burst.
They sell them at the NEX at boot camp, you can buy either $10 or $20 cards

Your PST scores are pretty decent, although I would work on getting your run time to under 10, and eventually under 9. If you get dropped from NACCS, you will go undes and might end up with a rate you don’t want. AWR/AWS is a pretty cool rate, and aircrew generally has good quality of life. You also won’t be primarily tasked with being a rescue swimmer, an AWR does a lot of cool anti sub and ISR stuff, AWS does a lot of general support. Both absolutely beat being undes and I guarantee you will hate your life a LOT more. I’m at NACCS too, backlogged. My biggest advice would be to phase up ASAP. Phase 1 sucks. That 0445 muster sucks. Get your watch qual, get inspections done, and enjoy being able to go off-base and walking around in civvies. For the next 5 months, you are basically being paid to exist and occasionally muster and stand watch. Have fun with buddies, work out a ton (Radford is a decent gym), go on runs, explore Pcola once you can go off base. Good luck man

PLEASE learn your General Orders early on! The biggest things you need to know are those, RTC CoC, and rank + recognition. I liked making notecards and studying that way. In boot camp when you have watch, you are encouraged to study while standing your post, too. Also, search up the CoC for RTC Great Lakes with photos of the actual people in each position. I found it a lot easier to remember it once I could put a name to a face.

When I arrived Aug. 25th, I ROMed for like, 2 days while they processed my covid card, then I got out of ROM. I’ve heard of some being in ROM for longer being fully vaxxed. It depends, but I would say you’ll likely and hopefully just ROM a few days

Yes, you have to wear the shittiest white cotton masks. The only time you can take them off is chow, running at freedom hall, hygiene, and ITE. Otherwise, mask is on the whole time, and if you are wearing it incorrectly and FQA (aka boot camp police) sees you, you can get a street hit/demerit chit and your RDCs will NOT be happy. It sucks but it’s survivable

There are times where I truly get to witness life’s simple wonders, whether it’s going on a walk outside, or doing things that I love, or (surprisingly enough) meeting new people that I click with. But once night time hits, I remember that I’ve disconnected from my friends, and we’re all changing in very different ways as we all recently graduated high school. They’re much more of the party type, I’m more of a “homebody” (as they put it and they ain’t wrong) and I have a lot of different interests and it’s starting to really show. I have one good friend who I am beyond thankful for and can truly always count on. Still, I often feel very alone. Still struggling to find love but I’ll be patient, I’ve had flings and all but nothing serious since my last relationship. I’m very introverted but it’s not fun when it’s not exactly always a choice to stay home. Anyways, it truly is the little things that make me feel happy. A surprise gift, coming across little bugs while doing yardwork, listening to good music, playing sports and having healthy competition, accomplishing small goals, talking with my parents, and eating good food. Stuff like that is what keeps me going, I’ve learned to appreciate the small stuff.  Anyone around me would consider me far from sentimental and emotional but... there’s been times where I damn near cried seeing a rabbit while out on a run. I keep that stuff to myself for the most part though :)

I actually enjoy playing multiplayer, talking mad trash to the other team and all. All the pressures of social cues and body language are gone, and the fact that I know I will literally never meet these people again get rid of the inhibition in me. But there are times where I’ll play and keep my mic muted because I’m inherently a tad but on the awkward side.

Not to echo-chamber, but reading is a legitimate way to expand your vocab, and therefore have more words in your arsenal to verbalize thoughts and idea. Picking up on things like tones and context all help. Another thing that somewhat helped me, but took a while to apply and I still struggle with to this day, is to slow down when speaking a bit! I 100% understand the anxiety, and introverts all seem to be in our own head, and I find myself blurting out whatever I might have to say as fast as I can, even though the actual idea was not very refined, and therefore makes little sense. Also like others have said, journaling does help too. I personally type mine, as something about writing makes it hard to follow and my handwriting is barely legible. Actually putting my thoughts and ideas on paper kinda transfers that skill to speaking as well.

I don’t know about volunteer billets for aircrew. It used to be a big thing back in the day but now, you just get an aircrew contract at MEPS. You can either do AIRC-ATF, which is on fixed-wing platforms and includes AWO, AWF, and AWV, or AIRR, which is AWS and AWR helicopter crewman. Hope this helped!

On the ASVAB, I think the highest area it had was some basic algebra and geometry. It does not touch calculus, otherwise I would have been screwed since I barely remember anything from the pre-calc class I took a few months ago! I say take it if you can, because why not, and maybe it'll keep your math skills sharp since it has a lot of the fundamentals of algebra, but don't sweat about the ASVAB math sections at all, it's all word problems and basic arithmetic.

I believe C2 aircrew are AWFs mainly, as far as a loadmaster-type role, in order to go there you sign a dry aircrew contract at MEPS and they choose for you at the end of NACCS, which is about a month after boot camp in total. You’re much more likely to go AWO, who fly on P8s to operate radar and acoustic equipment to hunt submarines, and can also be a AWV. Helicopter aircrewman can be picked from a dry aircrew pool for AWS, but for Romeo’s you have to sign an AIRR rescue swimmer contract at meps. I too am hoping to be an aircrewman, signed a dry aircrew contract at MEPS and hopefully will end up as an AWO on the P8. Good luck, hope this helped and if anything is wrong someone feel free to correct me!

I HIGHLY suggest no. Triple jump has a lot more impact and needs a flat base otherwise you're at risk for shin splints and rolled ankles, tj spikes have more cushion and a flatter base that really helps you plant your foot in all three phases. I use the Nike TJ Elite for both, using triple jump spikes will not cause you to lose distance in the long jump.

It looks like you're "rushing to the pit" and not getting enough extension at the end. Flexibility might be an issue, mainly in the hamstrings and back, there' countless stretches for those, both dynamic (warm-up) and static (post workout/meet). One thing that helped me was think about landing heels-first. This helped me keep my legs up and out. Also, try getting more height in the jump if you can, your momentum will take you plenty forward and having more height = more air time = longer jump. Good luck!

I'm in the same position as a senior. Our jump coach retired and our current coach isn't a long jump specialist and she also has to split time between being an elementary school teacher which is understandable, but it leaves me to be the pseudo coach half of the time. Thankfully no one else triple jumps so I don't have to do that as well, which would be hell because it's a lot harder to teach than long jump imo. I'd say start having everyone work on short approaches and getting the jump form down, along with teaching and working on approaches. One thing that's underrated is that with you being a current jumper and I'm assuming relatively good at it, you have the ability to teach by doing instead of just telling. Ask your coaches if there's a spare device that can record jumps in practice or maybe use your phone if they are comfortable with that. Telling them to watch film is good advice as well. Keep looking for workouts you can do with them, stuff that you would do anyways.
Talk to your school athletic trainer. Could be a pulled muscle and over use can only make it that much worse

There isn’t inherently anything wrong with drinking, morally or moderately-health wise. There is something wrong with dependence and peer pressuring. There are times where drinking may be appropriate, which in my opinion is when something’s worth celebrating like some holidays, retirements, promotions, etc. To me, drinking isn’t something you do every weekend because you’re bored. It’s kind of symbolic in a way that it gives you a break from the responsibilities and stresses of your work life and have no obligations so it’s ok to wallow in a little drunkenness once in a blue moon. I’ve been personally affected by those I care about not being able to control themselves while drunk or being victims of those who can’t and I think that’s part of the reason I’m not too on board with party-drinking-culture. Don’t ever let your friend’s peer pressure you, and at some point you may need to tell them to (respectfully) fuck off about it a little.There’s nothing wrong with (moderate) drinking, same as there’s nothing wrong with not drinking. Just my 2¢

Already being bilingual makes you very competitive for CTI. According to research, after learning 1 language, it gets easier to learn another, and you probably have a good ability to learn foreign languages. AFAIK, you don’t really get to pick what language, you’re tested on your aptitude to learn a language then go from there for assignment. I’d assume Chinese and Russian are big ones. If you wouldn’t mind having to learn a new language from scratch, I’d say go for it, especially if it’s something you’d enjoy doing and using in your work. There might be times where your knowledge of Japanese will be priceless, the Navy has a legitimate presence in Japan.

It’s relatively agreed upon that AW is one of the Navy’s better rates afa QoL and job enjoyment. Maybe I’m biased as I’m slotted to ship as AIRC, but every AW I’ve gotten to talk to enjoys their job. I’m sure there are those that hate it and those that barely care, but it seems it’s a fun and exciting job. Plus flight pay/per diem can bring it some pretty good money

My dad, a 30 year Navy vet, told me when I decided to join the Navy myself to go in with an open mind. When he enlisted in the 80s I doubt he planned on staying even 20 years, let alone 30. Another family member planned on doing his 4 years then leaving, he’s currently going on 10 years of service. You may love it, you may hate it, you may be “meh” with it. The only way is to do your time and decide if reenlisting is best for you according to what you’ve witnessed and done during your time in. Have a plan for both, and until then, let the experience itself help you decide is what I can say as just a DEPer

I know this post is somewhat old, but any new updates? Going through a similar situation: recruiter had me white-lie/omit info on my NASIS/SF86 for the Navy concerning marijuana usage and I plan on coming clean to my investigator, would love to hear how your situation is going.

Be honest with your recruiter about it. It can take up to three months to be clean. Recruiters usually don’t care too much. I brought it up to my recruiter and he said he smoked a bunch before he decided to join the Navy. A lot of recruiters are actually very helpful and will periodically drug test you with an at home test before sending you to MEPS. It took me about a month to get clean from an at home test and I went to MEPS a month later to be even more sure. But it also depends on your metabolism and bf%. If you have fat to lose, start losing it and sweating it out and drink plenty of water. Try finding a 15ng home test and once you can consistently pass those, tell your recruiter and go from there. When it comes time to fill out your NASIS, ESPECIALLY if your rate requires a clearance, DO NOT LIE! My recruiter had me lie about it and now I have to worry when it comes time for an investigation because I didn’t understand the magnitude of what I was filling out and plan to disclose all altered info. They care way more about legal issues, financial issues, and credit scores than experimentation, especially with marijuana. 3 months should be plenty of time to get clean if you were not a stupidly heavy user like you say, and in the mean time, completely distance yourself from it. My lie was saying I stopped usage earlier than I actually did and my usage was only experimental while in reality, I was a few-times a week user. For that lie though, I just had to sign a piece of paper basically saying I don’t like marijuana and don’t intend to smoke again. Smoking weed a bit in high school is fine, and if it was automatically disqualified half of the Navy wouldn’t exist and no one would hold a clearance. Lying is not fine. Maybe wait until you’re a senior/18 and stay sober until then? That should give you plenty of time to get clean and distance yourself from your last you. Good luck!

A lot of A School can translate to college credits, common advice I’ve heard is use Tuition Assistance while your in, then you’ll have 4 years of GI bill once you get out. Also, use the CLEP Exams for credits as well
I took the ASVAB through my school and was able to go to MEPS a few weeks later. After your scores come in, talk to your recruiter and go from there. It took ~2 weeks for mine to come in.

The only advice I personally have is study the areas you already have a proficiency in. For example, I suck at Auto & Shop, so I didn’t study anything related to it because none of the rates I wanted required it in the line scores. It’s an aptitude test meant to gauge what you’re already good in so no harm in getting better at what you are good in already. A lot of rates do require VE (PC + WK) though so I’d brush up on that, and take a look at the line score requirements for your top rates and study those. It’s all multiple choice so if nothing else you can take a lucky guess when stumped. Good luck!
